ld.description:
Daphne Gale is an indie-folk singer-songwriter whose work blends poetic lyricism, improvisational sensibility, and a deep connection to place. Raised in the Bronx and shaped by time spent farming in Vermont, her music moves between the pastoral and the metropolitan, the intimate and the expansive. With a background in opera and a grounding in folk tradition, she brings a rare emotional precision to both recording and live performance.

She has performed at venues including the Troubadour (Los Angeles), Le Poisson Rouge (New York), and Telluride Bluegrass Festival, and has collaborated and shared the stage with artists including Noah Kahan, Naomi Scott, Adam Melchor, and Taylor Ashton.

Her fourth album, COMPANY, will be released on November 11, 2026.

He leads the internationally acclaimed and award-winning Canzoniere Grecanico Salentino (founded in 1975 by Durante’s family), playing in all major world music festivals. ld.description:
Ballet is an ambient/experimental performance showcase based in Brooklyn, NY. This curation includes the US debut presentation of buttechno’s *endless Xpire*, Klein’s singular melding of noise and R&B, saxophonist Matana Roberts’ improvisational genius, and Significant Other’s debut live set via forthcoming audiovisual work.

buttechno's sonic identity is built on spacious, dystopian, and wonky reflections on techno that explore the liminal spaces between rhythm and texture. His productions feature rhythmic cells ranging from strict to rubbery, lending direction to blue, ruminating, and post-apocalyptic voids and creating soundscapes that mirror expansive barrenness and urban desolation. This approach has earned him recognition for providing "spastic electronics and fireball ballistics" at major festivals and legendary clubs.

Klein is an artist and musician whose work often blurs the lines between fact and fiction. Her music releases, films, and performances are often informed by urban mapping, surveillance, humor, hip-hop, noise, identity, and beyond. Her work has been shown and/or performed at museums, galleries, yards, squats, and pubs.

Matana Roberts \[they/them\] is a dynamic instrumentalist and multidisciplinary artist whose practice explores the mystical roots and intuitive, spirit-raising traditions of American creative expression. Their innovative work has forged new conceptual approaches to considering narrativity, history, and political expression within improvisatory structures.

Lesley Mok is a New York City-based percussionist, composer, and sound artist. Their work is guided by a continual search for the connection between the mundane and the divine, the experience and manipulation of time, and a desire to capture emotional dissonance and complexity. Drawing from American experimental music and the lineage of the AACM, Afro-Cuban folkloric traditions, drumline, and the sounds and textures of the natural environment, their practice moves fluidly between composition, improvisation, and electronic sound.

Significant Other, a UK-born DJ, producer, and curator now based in Berlin, has carved out a distinctive space in the electronic music landscape with his emotionally resonant productions and genre-resistant style of DJing. Consistently operating at the fringes, his creative output is an at-times chaotic fusion of the tough and more tender corners of modern dance music. Over the years, he has garnered a cult reputation for his take on the sludgier, atmospheric ends of contemporary mood-driven electronic music, including through his record label and Berlin event series Pain Management, an anti-dancefloor outlet for outsider sounds spanning spoken word, hellish dub experimentation, and avant-garde electronica: “body music for restless minds.”

ld.name: DURATIONS: Meredith Graves & Offal Literary Salon present Philosophy and Magic with Simon Critchley, Elvia Wilk, Joseph Earl Thomas, Sasha Ravitch

address.streetAddress: 233 Butler St, Brooklyn, NY 11217, USA

ld.description:
Magic, like philosophy, can be perfidious: it hides in plain sight, it re-writes systems of thinking, and it redesigns ways of being. Philosophy and the Occult Sciences are as much about concealing as they are revealing, and knowing when to do which. The true seat of power within any system is occupied by those individuals tasked with deciding who gets to see in the dark, who has access to the hidden tongues, what lies in wait on the Otherside – and perhaps most of all, by those who understand the two disciplines as perpetual strange bedfellows, at origin a monstrous two-headed birth still fighting any attempt at division well into the 21st century.

This year at Durations, in a special clandestine meeting of the Offal Salon, we aim to place a candle in front of a trick scrying mirror: four luminous writers from across genres and disciplinary specialties, whose work simultaneously conceals and reveals the inner workings \[in/of\] \[the/a\] machine, whether mechanical or human, with or without organs.

Join us on the evening of Friday November 13th for a series of individual readings followed by spirited conversation, and help us dissolve the lines between philosophy and magic, fiction and non-, meat and spirit.

Featuring:

Simon Critchley: Simon Critchley is the Hans Jonas Professor of Philosophy at The New School for Social Research and a Director of the Onassis Foundation. His work engages in many areas: continental philosophy, philosophy and literature, psychoanalysis, ethics, and political theory, among others. He has written over twenty books, including studies of Greek tragedy, David Bowie, football, suicide, Shakespeare, how philosophers die, and a novella. As co-editor of The Stone at the New York Times, Critchley showed that philosophy plays a vital role in the public realm. Additional information can be found at his personal website, simon-critchley.com.

Elvia Wilk: Elvia Wilk is the author of the novels Oval and A Diagnosis and the essay collection Death by Landscape. Her fiction, essays, and criticism appear in publications like Bookforum, Frieze, The New York Times, The New York Review of Books, The Atlantic, The Nation, WIRED, n+1, Granta, Conjunctions, BOMB, 4Columns, The Paris Review, and e-flux journal, where she is a contributing editor. Her work has been supported by the Andy Warhol Foundation, the Berggruen Institute, the Remarque Institute, Yaddo, the Hawthornden Foundation, Artlab, and La Becque, and she teaches in the MFA program at Sarah Lawrence College.

Joseph Earl Thomas: Joseph Earl Thomas is the author of Sink, A Memoir (Grand Central Publishing, 2023), longlisted for the PEN/Jean Stein Book Award, and shortlisted for the William Saroyan International Writing Prize; the novel God Bless You, Otis Spunkmeyer (Grand Central Publishing, 2024), longlisted for the Carnegie Medal for Literary Excellence, finalist for the LA Times Art Seidenbaum Award, winner of the Center for Fiction First Novel Prize; and the forthcoming story collection Leviathan Beach (Penguin Random House, 2027). His prose and poetry has been published or is forthcoming in The Kenyon Review, The Paris Review, The Verge, Harper’s, Virginia Quarterly Review, Vanity Fair, The Yale Review, The Massachusetts Review, and Dilettante Army. His honors include the 2020 Chautauqua Janus Prize, the Anisfield-Wolf Fellowship in Writing and Publishing, and fellowships from Kimbilio, VONA, Tin House and Bread Loaf. A graduate of the University of Notre Dame’s MFA program in prose, he earned his PhD in English from the University of Pennsylvania. He is a member of the writing faculty at Sarah Lawrence College as well as low residency MFA programs at Holy Family and Randolph Colleges, and teaches courses in Black Studies, Poetics, Video Games, Queer Theory and more at The Brooklyn Institute for Social Research.

Sasha Ravitch: Sasha Ravitch presents internationally at conferences, teaches classes and workshops, consults globally on witchcraft and occulture, and writes fiction, theory, and creative non-fiction. Having pioneered a field of witchcraft informed by cosmic horror and posthumanist and post-Lacanian critical theory, the resultant non-fiction manuscript is forthcoming with Revelore Press. She’s been published by Brooklyn Rail, Weirdpunk Books, Strange Horizons, hex literary, and more, and is a former Banff Centre for Arts & Creativity residency recipient, and McCormack Writing Center (formerly Tin House) Oregon Summer Workshop alum. Ravitch is the co-founder and EIC for antilogos press, founder and curator of offal literary salon salon, and her current hyperfixation is the Semiotic Realm and the Bakhtin-Kristevan concept of “the carnival” within the context of fandom internet thirdspaces.

ld.name: DURATIONS: An Evening with Terre Thaemlitz [Live Piano] + Conversation with Ciarán Finlayson - at Roulette Intermedium

address.streetAddress: 233 Butler St, Brooklyn, NY 11217, USA

ld.description:
Presented in collaboration with Triple Canopy at Roulette Intermedium.

The performance will be followed by a conversation with Triple Canopy contributing editor Ciarán Finlayson, who will speak with Thaemlitz about her music as well as her criticism, which often takes up the defects of a culture industry that offers artists “exposure” instead of wages.

Starting in 2024, Terre Thaemlitz began a new series of durational piano solo performances. Unlike Thaemlitz's computer-composed Rubato Series digital piano concerts of the past, these current performances are acoustic and played on a grand piano (180 cm or larger). Each show consists of a new composition using improvisational systems, with occasional prepared-piano techniques. While sonically more dynamic than Thaemlitz's notorious 32-hour-long acoustic piano piece, \*Meditation on Wage Labor and the Death of the Album\* (2012), this new series continues the minimalist, ambient, and neo-expressionist piano playing developed over the past three decades in Thaemlitz's various electroacoustic and house albums.

The first performance of this series took place in June 2024, as a close to Trajal Harrell's five-year stint as resident choreographer at the Schauspielhaus Zürich. Both Harrell and Thaemlitz have their own histories within the US voguing ball scene, and both have continually examined the tensions between culturally minor and major audio movements. On that night, Harrell gave the final performance of her acclaimed group choreography for Keith Jarrett's \*Köln Concert\*, followed by what was lightheartedly billed as Thaemlitz's "Zürich Concert." Thaemlitz's longtime collaborator Mark Fell was quick to note, "You're no Keith Jarrett"—the stylistic and ideological incongruities between Jarrett and Thaemlitz being the point.

The performances are not recorded, streamed, or archived. This is in keeping with Thaemlitz's longstanding no-recording policy, rooted in a critical rejection of today's homogenizing archive industries. This policy began in the early 2010s, in specific reaction to sudden federal and corporate financial interests in building LGBT archives, which went against Thaemlitz's own strategies of the closet, invisibility, secrecy, withholding, and remaining culturally minor. It is also a means of interfering with the audio market's and audiences' tendencies to fetishize recordings of Jarrett-style "you had to be there" performances. Rather, Thaemlitz privately records the preparatory sessions leading up to each show. These will eventually be self-released through Comatonse Recordings as collections containing four to five separate takes, giving a sense of what happened at the live performances while still refusing to settle on a single take as "the one."

Triple Canopy is committed to cultivating unconventional, unassimilated forms of thought and expression, and to meaningfully supporting the people who produce them. The magazine collaborates with contributors on artworks, essays, fictions, conversations, performances, and books \[among other media\] from conception to realization, navigating the digital and physical realms where ideas and audiences take shape. In doing so, Triple Canopy strives to not only analyze but alter the structures that influence whose voices are heard, whose stories are circulated, and whose experiences are valued.

Founded in 2007 and based in New York City, Triple Canopy is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization, has been certified by W.A.G.E., and is a member of the Coalition of Small Arts New York City (CoSA NYC).

ld.description:
With origins in the American South, All Get Out fuse indie rock and emo punk, merging the melodic warmth and intensity of Band of Horses and My Morning Jacket with the raw, insistent singing style of Modest Mouse and Manchester Orchestra.

Their approach paired melodic guitar lines with propulsive rhythms that underscored often confessional and unsparing lyrics. Following the first self-titled debut in 2008, they delivered 2011’s The Season, which earned cult status within indie and emo circles. Even after that breakthrough, the band stayed largely inactive for several years while reassessing the project’s direction.

All Get Out resurfaced in 2015 with the Movement EP. They promptly issued Nobody Likes a Quitter on Favorite Gentlemen/Bad Timing Records in 2016, an album produced and co-written with Manchester Orchestra’s Andy Hull and Robert McDowell. The resulting fourth album, No Bouquet on Equal Vision, appeared in 2018. As the decade closed, the duo issued additional material, including the 2019 Northport Sessions EP, an Audiotree Live EP, and a 2021 acoustic reinterpretation of The Season marking its tenth anniversary.

Turning toward a fresh chapter, All Get Out unveiled their fifth album, Kodak, in 2022, marking a deliberate change in course. They extended that trajectory on the swift follow-up, the second self-titled LP All Get Out in 2023, which wove folk, emo, and Americana elements into an expanded palette that broadened their songwriting range.

ld.description:
EARLY SHOW ADDED DUE TO DEMAND

**Emma Ruth Rundle** made a conscious choice to reach towards making a hopeful record for the follow up to 2021’s *Engine of Hell*. Where outside forces tempted her to turn inwards, towards isolation and hopelessness, she instead reached outwards to create a record that acknowledges pain, but offers both community and resilience in response. Although *These Killing Times* possesses a spirit of defiance, it retains the tenderness and vulnerability that saw her earlier work resonate with so many listeners.

*These Killing Times* is electrifying, emotional, and charged with feminine rage; it is a reactive anthology, bristling, full of life and full of resistance - forged by and for community. It asks many questions - of the roles we play as individuals, or as artists - and closes with this one: what will we live for beyond the valley of the shadow of the fear of all men? A question with no definitive answer as yet, but one that is being asked with increasing urgency - here on this record, and beyond.

**Cinder Well** is the musical project of Los Angeles–based songwriter, composer, and multi-instrumentalist Amelia Baker. Cinder Well extracts dark, rich and tender compositions which nod to, but also stray from traditional musical languages.

ld.description:
Karachi Community Radio Presents YOUNG STUNNERS & Jokhay, in collaboration with RM Live for their debut New York show.

Young Stunners are among the defining voices of contemporary South Asian hip-hop. Formed in Karachi in 2012 by Talha Anjum and Talhah Yunus, the duo has helped transform Urdu rap from an underground movement into a powerful force in Pakistan’s mainstream music culture and across the South Asian diaspora. Moving effortlessly between Urdu and English, they blend intricate lyricism, sharp social observation and contemporary production to create music that feels both deeply local and universally relatable. Early releases like Burger-e-Karachi brought an irreverent, distinctly Pakistani perspective to rap, while later songs such as Gumaan, Afsanay, Laga Reh and Why showcased their range, from hard-hitting verses to emotionally vulnerable songwriting.

Working closely with producer Jokhay, the duo has built a recognizable sound defined by atmospheric production and lyric-driven storytelling. Their reach extends well beyond independent hip-hop, with high-profile moments including the Pakistan Super League anthem Groove Mera and Coke Studio Season 14’s Phir Milenge, alongside Faisal Kapadia. More than a musical act, Young Stunners represent a generational shift in how South Asian artists create and share their work, proving that language is no barrier to global connection and that artists can reach audiences worldwide without leaving their cultural identities behind.

About Karachi Community Radio (KCR)

Established in 2017, Karachi Community Radio operates as a community-driven project with a focus on archiving, promoting, and advancing contemporary music and art. Our intervention of sound and space is dedicated to the cultivation and expansion of the electronic music and DIY experimental audio-visual scene, particularly from a South Asian perspective. Over the years, KCR has extended its influence on a global scale, gaining recognition for producing Pakistan’s first "Boiler Room" event, which has garnered millions of views worldwide. Additionally, KCR has produced visuals for Glastonbury Festival, Ultra, Coachella and curated projects for prestigious platforms such as Elsewhere, SILO, Public Records, Karachi Biennale, Cannes Film Festival, Lot Radio, Dub Lab, among others.

ld.name: Nero (DJ Set)

address.streetAddress: 90 Scott Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11237, USA

ld.description:
“Love will always still exist,” insists NERO front-woman Alana Watson. “Far into the future, when all that remains is rubble and destruction, there’ll be that shaft of light coming up through the ruins.”

Grammy Award-winning, Ivor Novello-nominated trio NERO return this year with an album that celebrates that sense of love among the ruins, and cements their reputation as one of Britain’s most exciting bands. It both complements 2012’s Number One album ‘Welcome Reality’ (and attendant hits ‘Me & You’, ‘Guilt’ and the chart-topping smash ‘Promises’) and pushes the band’s apocalyptic and frequently romantic electronic sound further than ever before. As ‘Into The Past’, their 2013 contribution to Baz Luhrmann’s Great Gatsby soundtrack hinted, and their 2015 Coachella headline slot proved, the now fully formed three-piece are more finely tuned now than ever before.

Completed in London during the spring of 2015, ‘Between II Worlds’ began life three years ago in LA, in the Hollywood Hills house where Orson Welles wrote Citizen Kane. Magnificent set up single ‘The Thrill’ was the first song the band wrote during those sessions. “We must have rewritten it 100 times after that,” smiles Dan Stephens who, alongside Joe Ray, founded NERO in 2004. “And inevitably we ended up going straight back to the first version.” Adds Joe: “If you’ve been working on a track for that long and it still flicks your switches, you know where must be something about it.”

‘The Thrill’ is a striking example of how far the band’s songwriting has progressed but the super-stylised, bass-heavy sound is unmistakably NERO, even if the styles and influences that pepper the band’s back catalogue – from classical, to rave, to drum ’n’ bass, dubstep and pop – mean the Nero sound often defies categorisation. “We’ve always liked pop craft in terms of song structure,” Dan says, “but it’s a constant battle to make that work with electronic and dance elements.”

It’s a battle that’s paid off – and as the title ‘Between II Worlds’ suggests, that’s not the only conflict at the heart of NERO’S new music. Alana’s often fragile vocals provide a brilliantly hypnotic foil to Dan and Joe’s uncompromising, hard-edged production, while that production is informed by an enigmatic retro-futuristic ideology, with its nods to Ridley Scott’s vision of a decrepit future in Blade Runner, that runs through the band’s entire identity. And then, of course, there’s that love in the ruins: the glimmer of hope in the most brutal setting.

The release of ‘Between II Worlds’ marks NERO stepping slightly out of the shadows, with Alana front and centre like never before. In fact ‘Welcome Reality’ took shape Alana was working as a midwife — a position she still held when ‘Promises’ hit Number One. “I had that 40+-hour-a-week job and all my days off were spent recording and gigging,” she recalls. Dan feels the shift in focus is a significant step. “Not many electronic acts have just one singer, but we always wanted to go out like a band,” he says, adding with a laugh: “It’s especially nice as Joe and I can just blend into the background.”

This progression might have seemed unimaginable to the two chaps who’d each experimented with electronic music on their own, and first met through mutual friends in north London fifteen years ago. Before long they’d become regulars at nights like Fabric’s Friday night True Playaz parties, and soon the music they made together became part of those sets. In, 2010 they signed to Chase & Status’ MTA label. After that things started happening quickly, though not without the occasional hitch — their first radio play came when Zane Lowe played a 45rpm dubplate at the wrong speed. “He played it at the right speed the next night,” Joe laughs, “then announced that he preferred it at 33, so played it at the wrong speed again.”

NERO originally materialised at a strange time — when all the producers around them were embracing new technology so wholeheartedly that their old equipment ended its days on eBay. “Dance music went digital and so did the equipment,” Joe remembers. “The thing is, you might have all the newest technology, but you want the old sounds as well.” Flash-forward a decade and that belief remains at the heart of Nero’s setup: ‘Between II Worlds’ was recorded using state-of-the-art software but also gorgeous, clapped-out synth relics — Roland Jupiter 8s, Yamaha CS-80 — that malfunction if the air conditioning packs in. “The synths are like a classic car – they go wrong quite a lot,” Dan smiles. “But that’s what can be missing from electronic music: a feeling of being organic, that some things are variable, and that sometimes things goes a bit wrong.”

That sense of the imperfect human influence, and an imperfect future built by human hands, is integral to NERO’S vision. As Dan notes: “We love that Blade Runner view of a future that’s bleak, and it’s raining and there’s smoke, and where even modern technology seems quite retro.” It was actually fans, rather than the band, who first decided that NERO’S debut album was set in a desolate future world. But it’s a theme the band subsequently threw themselves into and ‘Between II Worlds’ continues a motif established all the way back in the band’s ‘Innocence’ video, which was inspired by the Manga film Cyber City Oedo 808. The film was set in the year 2808 — that year was then referenced in ‘Doomsday’, and it’s also there in the ‘Me & You’ video. In 2011 the band’s groundbreaking collaboration with the BBC Philharmonic Orchestra was dubbed the 2808 Symphony, and when Nero first teased fans with news of ‘Between II Worlds’, they did so on SoundCloud with an uploaded piece of music whose length was 28:08. Single Satisfy quickly followed said piece of music, swiftly being added to the Radio 1 A List. The concept continues now with the release date of ‘Between II Worlds’ on 28/08. (“It doesn’t work so well in America,” Alana accepts.)

The strikingly visual element to Nero’s music has led to numerous soundtrack requests of the last few years — Joe is only half joking when he says they’re holding out for Blade Runner 2, but they did make time for Baz Luhrmann’s production of The Great Gatsby. Luhrmann had originally used Nero’s old song ‘Departure’ on the film, but that song now appears in its third (and the band promise final) iteration on ‘Between II Worlds’.

Elsewhere on the album ‘Two Minds’ is a thunderous belter half a decade in the making (Alana wrote her part five years ago, but it wasn’t until recently that Dan and Joe came up with music that matched the song), while ‘It Comes And Goes’ is a song Joe wrote inspired by the likes of The Streets and Burial. “It’s about that feeling at the end of the night when you’re leaving a rave,” Joe says. “With lines like ‘the night time’s the hardest time and it knows all my lies’ we wanted to push the limits of how poetic you could get on a dance track.”

Actually, ‘Between II Worlds’ as a whole is a uniquely persuasive example of how totally boundless dance music can and always should be. “Musically we’ve always been into the idea of a journey, whether it’s through an album or a DJ set,” Dan explains. “On the album, ’Into The Night’ and ‘What Does Love Mean’ are both about an escape: you don’t know what they’re escaping, but they’re both about taking a journey. There are hints at a story with no beginning or end: just snapshots.”

NERO may be enigmatic, but the snapshots scattered throughout ‘Between II Worlds’ build a picture of a band entering an exciting new phase. And it’s a phase that celebrates intense but accessible songwriting alongside the myriad musical styles that continue to inform the NERO sound.

“People talk about genres a lot,” Dan explains. “But for NERO it’s never been about any genres. It’s about electronic music, and it’s about us.”

ld.description:
***Jonathan Something is no stranger to transformation. Born Jonathan Searles in Brooklyn, CT, the critically acclaimed songwriter has shed his creative skin repeatedly, disappearing for years at a time only to return with a radically reimagined sound and fresh lyrical perspective on each successive record. But even for a lifelong chameleon, Searles’ mesmerizing new album, One More Lonesome Cowboy Song, marks a radical departure.***

***Recorded and produced by Searles, who also plays all of the instruments, the collection is gentle and hypnotic, with an intimate, understated delivery that’s at once aching and beautiful. The songwriting is indeed rooted in the cosmic cowboy tradition of Gram Parsons or Gene Clark, but the recordings share more in common with Neutral Milk Hotel or Elliott Smith, layering up fingerpicked acoustic and electric guitars with hushed, serenely doubletracked vocals. The result is an album that feels both lush and raw at the same time, a captivating inner monologue of a record that finds comfort in slowing down, tuning in, and making peace with the moment.***

***One More Lonesome Cowboy Song follows an eclectic series of early albums that ranged in style from blistering garage rock and quirky anti-folk to retro synthpop and sample-laden neo-soul, prompting NPR’s Slingshot series to hail Searles’ “delightfully bizarre” approach and The Line of Best Fit to declare that “he’s thrown out whatever rulebook he went by (if there ever was one).”***

***Four years ago, in a vastly different context, Cafuné—the indie-pop powerhouse of Noah Yoo and Sedona Schat—released Running, a bionic debut album that soundtracked a collective urge for post-pandemic escapism. That record, Schat says, “is literally all about running away.” But as the duo enters its tenth year, their foundational questions—of authenticity, artificiality, and the existential tension between the two—feel more pressing than ever. “The entire time that the band has existed,” Schat says, “it’s always been about negotiating between digital manipulation and raw realness.”***

***This moment—one increasingly defined by AI, algorithms, and artificial intimacy—is very much a bastion of “digital manipulation” in itself. Recorded in 2024, their new record finds the band at a familiar crossroads, reckoning between real and fake. The difference, this time around, is that they’re doing it in the real world, too. And it sounds like it. Bite Reality captures Cafuné in a confrontational state, no longer running from the bite of reality, but biting reality back. Their guitars growl; their vocals snarl; their lyrics teem with brutal honesty, not avoidant analogy. “Self-flagellation is not cute after a certain point,” Yoo says, with a laugh. “That’s not even helpful,” Schat adds. “What helps you to be better is actually facing: What is really wrong, and how do I work through it?”***

***Bite Reality is about the fine line between documenting your existence and doing the work to actually exist. What does humanity look, sound, and feel like in a dehumanizing era? Why prove that you’re alive when you can just live?***
